title: Anne of Green Gables
author: L. M. Montgomery
setting: Avonlea, a farming village on the north shore of Prince Edward Island, in the 1890s
lengthNote: Thirty-eight chapters, each one shaped like a complete episode
openingLine: Mrs. Rachel Lynde lived just where the Avonlea main road dipped down into a little hollow, fringed with alders and ladies’ eardrops and traversed by a brook that had its source away back in the woods of the old Cuthbert place.
summary: Two elderly unmarried siblings send to an orphan asylum for a boy to help on the farm and are sent a talkative eleven-year-old girl instead. What follows is not a story about a child charming everybody, but about the slow and often reluctant conversion of a household and a village: Marilla learns to say what she feels only when it is nearly too late, and Anne learns which of her gifts are worth keeping. Montgomery puts the comedy of a broken slate and a green-dyed head beside a bereavement and a narrowed future, and lets the second give the first its weight.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Anne of Green Gables
sourceText.note: The thirty-eight chapters are numbered I to XXXVIII in the text and cited here by Arabic numeral. The base text is the 1908 first edition, with its American spelling and punctuation.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: L. C. Page and Company of Boston, after Montgomery signed with the firm in April 1907.

atAGlance.label: Written at
atAGlance.note: Montgomery began the novel in June 1905 in the house where her grandparents had brought her up.

atAGlance.label: The premise
atAGlance.note: An elderly couple apply to an orphanage for a boy and are sent a girl by mistake.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Roughly five years, counted in seasons, concerts, examinations and mistakes.

structure.label: Chapters 1–6
structure.title: The mistake, and Marilla keeps Anne
structure.summary: Mrs Rachel Lynde sees Matthew drive past in his good clothes and goes to find out why. At Bright River a small girl is waiting on a pile of shingles, and by the time Marilla has decided that the mistake must be corrected, the alternative — a hard-worked household at Mrs Blewett’s — has shown her what correcting it would mean.

structure.label: Chapters 7–12
structure.title: Bringing-up begun
structure.summary: Anne is taught to say her prayers, offends Mrs Rachel Lynde about her hair and freckles, and refuses to apologise until an apology can be performed with full dramatic satisfaction. Sunday school, a wreath of buttercups on a hat, and the vow of eternal friendship with Diana Barry all belong to this stretch.

structure.label: Chapters 13–18
structure.title: School, Diana and the boy with the slate
structure.summary: Anne confesses to a theft she did not commit in order to attend a picnic, breaks a slate over Gilbert Blythe’s head for calling her carrots, and accidentally makes Diana drunk on Marilla’s currant wine. The croup night at the Barrys’ ends the estrangement and establishes Anne as useful in an emergency.

structure.label: Chapters 19–23
structure.title: A run of catastrophes
structure.summary: The Haunted Wood terrifies its own inventor, the liniment cake ruins a minister’s tea, and a dare on Mr Barry’s kitchen roof ends with a sprained ankle. Each disaster is also an introduction: Aunt Josephine, Mrs Allan and a village that begins to take Anne’s part.

structure.label: Chapters 24–29
structure.title: Puffed sleeves, green hair and the lily maid
structure.summary: Miss Stacy arrives and changes what school can be; Matthew, after a lengthy campaign of embarrassment, buys a dress with puffed sleeves. Anne dyes her hair green, has it cut off, and nearly drowns playing Tennyson’s Elaine — and is pulled out of the water by Gilbert Blythe, whose apology she still will not accept.

structure.label: Chapters 30–36
structure.title: Queen’s, the pass list and the Avery
structure.summary: The Queen’s class is organised, Anne and Gilbert tie for first place on the entrance list, and a year in Charlottetown ends with the Avery scholarship and the prospect of a B.A. Marilla and Matthew are proud in their separate, largely silent ways, and Matthew says the one thing he has never said.

structure.label: Chapters 37–38
structure.title: Matthew’s death, and the bend in the road
structure.summary: A bank fails, Matthew dies of the shock, and Marilla learns that her eyes will not stand much more use. Anne gives up the scholarship, takes the Avonlea school, and makes her peace with Gilbert at a gate; the novel ends with a road that no longer runs straight.

characters.name: Anne Shirley
characters.role: An eleven-year-old sent by mistake to Green Gables
characters.summary: She arrives with a carpet-bag, a vocabulary out of borrowed books and a history of minding other people’s babies, and her talk is the only property she has ever been allowed to keep. The novel is careful never to cure her of imagination, only to teach her when it clarifies a thing and when it hides one that needs attention.
characters.clue: She renames a pond, a road and an avenue on the drive from the station, refuses to answer to a name spelled without its last letter, and once walked a ridgepole on a dare.
traits: unable to leave a name unimproved

characters.name: Marilla Cuthbert
characters.summary: Practical, sarcastic and frightened of her own affections, she is the character the novel actually changes. Montgomery gives her the funniest dry lines and then, in the last two chapters, the admission that she has never found it easy to say anything out of her heart — which is why the saying of it lands so hard.
characters.clue: She keeps her brooch in a drawer and her feelings further back than that, and her first recorded reaction to a strange child in her kitchen is to ask where the boy is.

characters.name: Matthew Cuthbert
characters.role: Marilla’s brother, a farmer afraid of women
characters.summary: He is frightened of everyone except Anne and says almost nothing to anybody, which makes the four or five sentences he does say the emotional pivots of the book. His campaign to buy a dress with puffed sleeves is comedy; his remark about a dozen boys is the reason the last chapters work.
characters.clue: Shy to the point of illness with any woman but his sister, he drives to the station in his best clothes, cannot bring himself to correct a mistake, and later buys brown sugar by accident while trying to buy a dress.
traits: the first to take her side

characters.name: Diana Barry
characters.summary: Pretty, good-natured and entirely without imagination, she is the ordinary against which Anne is measured and the first person ever to want Anne’s company for its own sake. The friendship survives being forbidden, which is more than most of the novel’s adult relationships are asked to do.
characters.clue: She is the only other girl of the right age at the right end of Avonlea, she is made drunk on three tumblers of what she thinks is cordial, and her mother forbids the friendship for a season.

characters.name: Gilbert Blythe
characters.role: The best scholar in Avonlea school
characters.summary: He calls Anne carrots in Chapter 15 and spends the rest of the novel paying for it, first with a broken slate and then with five years of refused apologies. Montgomery keeps him mostly offstage, so the rivalry spurs Anne’s ambition and does not become a romance.
characters.clue: He pulls a girl out of the river after her leaky flat sinks, and she thanks him and then declines to forgive him for something he said when they were thirteen.

characters.name: Mrs Rachel Lynde
characters.summary: She runs the Sewing Circle, the Church Aid Society and, in practice, the village’s opinion of itself, and the book opens by describing a brook that behaves itself as it passes her window. Her quarrel with Anne over red hair and freckles is the first test of whether Avonlea will treat a child as a character or a case.
characters.clue: Sixteen cotton-warp quilts, a kitchen window over the main road, and an opinion delivered to a strange child’s face about her skinniness, her freckles and her hair.

characters.name: Miss Stacy
characters.role: The new teacher at Avonlea school
characters.summary: She takes the pupils into the woods, gets up concerts, and organises the Queen’s class that gives Anne a route out of the village. She is the book’s picture of what a good teacher does — she does not tame ambition, she gives it an examination timetable.
characters.clue: Field days, recitations and physical culture arrive with her, and the Avonlea parents are not sure about any of it until the pass list appears in the paper.

characters.name: Miss Josephine Barry
characters.summary: Two children jump into her bed in the dark and she becomes, improbably, one of Anne’s allies, the first adult outside Green Gables to be won over by talk. She provides the tea-parties, the concert tickets and the second home in town that the last chapters need.
characters.clue: Rich, easily offended and staying in the spare room, she is landed on in the dark by two girls racing for the spare-room bed.

themes.name: Belonging
themes.summary: Anne arrives as a clerical error and spends the first six chapters not knowing whether she will be sent back, and the novel never lets the reader forget the alternative: Mrs Blewett’s household, where a child would be a pair of hands. Belonging here is decided by adults in kitchens, and it has to be decided again each time Anne does something disastrous.
themes.development: A mistake in Chapter 3, a decision in Chapter 6, a conditional welcome for twenty chapters, and finally Marilla saying it aloud when the household has nothing else left.

themes.name: Imagination
themes.summary: Anne’s imagination is a way of living inside material limits: nothing else she owns can make a pond into the Lake of Shining Waters. The book is unusual in insisting that the same faculty is dangerous — it produces the Haunted Wood she cannot walk through, the hair dye she believes in and the Elaine who nearly drowns.
themes.development: A defence against the asylum in the early chapters, a social gift by the middle of the book, and by Queen’s a thing she can switch off long enough to pass an examination.

themes.name: Names
themes.summary: Anne’s first act at Green Gables is to negotiate the spelling of her own name, and her second is to rename the neighbourhood. For a child whose clothes, placements and prospects have all been decided elsewhere, naming is the one power she has, and Montgomery treats it as a serious claim.
themes.development: Cordelia and the e in Chapter 3, the Lake of Shining Waters and the White Way of Delight on the drive, and at the end the names have stuck: the village uses them too.

themes.name: Orphans, hired help and respectable farms
themes.summary: The novel is exact about money and position without saying so: a boy from an asylum is labour, a girl is a liability, Mrs Blewett wants someone to mind her children, and the Cuthberts’ respectability makes Green Gables a different proposition. The bank failure in the last chapters shows how narrow that margin of respectability actually is.
themes.development: An asylum and a farm in Chapter 6, hand-me-down wincey dresses against puffed sleeves in Chapter 25, and a scholarship given up for a mortgage-free house in Chapter 38.

themes.name: School, scholarship and ambition
themes.summary: Ambition in this book is specific and measurable — a pass list in the paper, a First Class licence, the Avery scholarship, a B.A. — and it belongs to a girl in a farming village in the 1890s. Miss Stacy does not soften it; she organises it, and the rivalry with Gilbert is the engine.
themes.development: A broken slate in Chapter 15, a class organised in Chapter 30, a tie at the head of the pass list, and then an ambition that has to be recalculated and is not given up.

themes.name: Grief and sacrifice
themes.summary: The last two chapters withdraw almost everything the book has been building: Matthew dies, Marilla’s sight is failing, and the scholarship goes to somebody else. Montgomery refuses both the tragic ending and the consolation prize, and has Anne argue that a narrowed road is not a closed one.
themes.development: A bank failure and a death in Chapter 37, a decision in Chapter 38, and a last paragraph in which the horizon has come in and the happiness is described as quiet.

techniques.name: Free indirect style
techniques.definition: Third-person narration that slips into a character’s own idiom without announcing that it is doing so.
techniques.inThisBook: The narration shifts into Marilla’s vocabulary at the moments she would never speak aloud — worrying about what Mrs Rachel will say, admitting to herself that the house has changed — which is how a character who says almost nothing becomes the book’s second centre.

techniques.name: Idiolect
techniques.definition: Giving each character a distinct and consistent way of speaking.
techniques.inThisBook: Anne speaks in paragraphs, with subordinate clauses and italics; Matthew begins almost every sentence with ‘Well now’; Marilla answers in one flat line. A page of dialogue needs almost no attribution.

techniques.name: Narratorial irony
techniques.definition: A narrator whose tone judges what it reports without saying so.
techniques.inThisBook: The first page describes a brook that grows well-conducted as it passes Mrs Rachel Lynde’s window — the village’s power over its inhabitants stated as a fact about hydrology before a single person has spoken.

techniques.name: Allusion
techniques.definition: Quotation or reference used to enlarge, or to puncture, the scene at hand.
techniques.inThisBook: Anne stages Tennyson’s Elaine in a leaky flat and nearly drowns, recites ‘The Dog at His Master’s Grave’ at Sunday school, and closes the novel with a line of Browning — her reading is always trying to convert Avonlea into something more like a poem.

techniques.name: The comic set piece
techniques.definition: A self-contained episode built to a single disaster, complete in one chapter.
techniques.inThisBook: The liniment cake, the currant wine, the dyed hair and the ridgepole each occupy a chapter, end in humiliation, and leave one permanent change behind — a new ally, a lesson, or a piece of Avonlea folklore.

techniques.name: The year as structure
techniques.definition: Organising the story’s time by the seasons and recurring village events, not by plot.
techniques.inThisBook: Blossom, harvest, the Sunday-school picnic, the winter concert and the examination timetable mark the passage of five years; chapters end with weather as often as with incident.

quotations.text: not even a brook could run past Mrs. Rachel Lynde’s door without due regard for decency and decorum
quotations.context: The opening sentence of the novel, describing the hollow where Mrs Rachel lives.
quotations.analysis: A brook that is headlong and full of dark secrets in the woods becomes quiet and well-conducted when it reaches a particular window: the village’s disciplinary power is established as a fact of the landscape before any character speaks. The alliteration of ‘decency and decorum’ is Mrs Rachel’s own phrasing, lent to the narrator a paragraph before she is introduced.

quotations.text: I asked her to go into the ladies’ waiting room, but she informed me gravely that she preferred to stay outside. ‘There was more scope for imagination,’ she said. She’s a case, I should say.
quotations.speaker: The station master
quotations.context: Matthew arrives at Bright River to collect a boy and is told what is waiting for him.
quotations.analysis: Anne’s defining phrase reaches the reader at second hand, inside a railwayman’s report, with quotation marks around it as though it were evidence. ‘She’s a case’ is the verdict Avonlea will keep offering for thirty chapters, and the novel’s method is to let her phrase outlive the judgement.

quotations.text: I shall call it⁠—let me see⁠—the Lake of Shining Waters. Yes, that is the right name for it. I know because of the thrill.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: On the drive from Bright River, renaming Barry’s pond.
quotations.analysis: The test she applies is physical: a name is right when it gives her a thrill, which makes naming a kind of instrument reading. Note that she does this before she knows whether she is allowed to stay — the renaming of the district is done by a child who may be sent back on the morning train.

quotations.text: But if you call me Anne please call me Anne spelled with an e.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: In the Green Gables kitchen, being questioned by Marilla about the mistake.
quotations.analysis: The sentence concedes and demands in the same breath: she gives up Cordelia and instantly opens a second negotiation. A child with no say over where she sleeps is bargaining over orthography, which is the only territory available to her, and the request is granted — Marilla uses the formula back at her twice in the same scene.

quotations.text: When you hear a name pronounced can’t you always see it in your mind, just as if it was printed out? I can; and A-n-n looks dreadful, but A-n-n-e looks so much more distinguished.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Explaining to Marilla why the letter matters.
quotations.analysis: The explanation is an accurate description of synaesthetic reading, offered by a child to an adult who has never thought about it. It also sets up the difference between them: Marilla hears words, Anne sees them printed, and most of their misunderstandings for the next thirty chapters follow from that.

quotations.text: I can’t. I’m in the depths of despair. Can you eat when you are in the depths of despair?
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Refusing supper on her first evening, having been told she is not wanted.
quotations.analysis: The phrase is borrowed from books and used with complete sincerity, and the question that follows is genuine — she is asking for information. Marilla’s flat reply, that she has never been in the depths of despair, sets the two registers of the novel against each other in three lines of dialogue.

quotations.text: “We might be some good to her,” said Matthew suddenly and unexpectedly.
quotations.speaker: Matthew Cuthbert
quotations.context: Marilla has been listing the reasons the child cannot possibly stay.
quotations.analysis: Seven words that decide the book, and the narrator draws attention to their rarity: ‘suddenly and unexpectedly’ is about Matthew speaking at all. The grammar also reverses the household’s assumption: they had applied for a boy who would be some good to them.

quotations.text: Suppose she wasn’t really going to stay here! She would imagine she was. There was scope for imagination here.
quotations.context: Anne’s first morning, kneeling at the east gable window.
quotations.analysis: Free indirect style puts the reader inside a decision being made in real time: the exclamation is Anne’s, and so is the flat sentence that answers it. Imagination here is a deliberate act of management: she will imagine that she is staying because the alternative is unbearable and she has nothing else to fall back on.

quotations.text: A bosom friend⁠—an intimate friend, you know⁠—a really kindred spirit to whom I can confide my inmost soul.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Explaining to Marilla what she means when she says she wants a bosom friend.
quotations.analysis: The definition arrives in three stages, each one more literary than the last, and the escalation is the joke. But the sentence also names the novel’s scarcest commodity: Anne has had households, matrons and other people’s twins, and has never once had a person of her own choosing.

quotations.text: It would be so much easier to be good if one’s hair was a handsome auburn, don’t you think?
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: To Mrs Rachel Lynde, immediately after making her apology for the quarrel about her looks.
quotations.analysis: The apology has just been performed with theatrical relish, and this is the sentence that follows it: goodness treated as a matter of appearance, offered to the woman whose remark about her hair caused the quarrel. Montgomery lets Anne win Mrs Rachel over in the same speech in which she reveals she has learned nothing about vanity.

quotations.text: “Carrots! Carrots!”
quotations.speaker: Gilbert Blythe
quotations.context: In the schoolroom, after Gilbert has failed to make Anne look at him.
quotations.analysis: Two words, one line to itself, and five years of plot. The word is an insult about poverty as much as about colour — red hair is the one feature of herself Anne has never been able to reimagine — and it arrives from the only pupil in Avonlea who is her intellectual equal.

quotations.text: “There’s a great deal of difference between being called a crow and being called carrots,” said Anne with dignity. “Gilbert Blythe has hurt my feelings excruciatingly, Diana.”
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Diana has pointed out that Charlie Sloane calls her a crow and she does not mind.
quotations.analysis: ‘With dignity’ is the narrator’s small betrayal of a girl who has just broken a slate over a boy’s head, and ‘excruciatingly’ is Anne restoring the scale of the injury by vocabulary alone. The distinction she is defending is real to her and invisible to everyone else, which is the shape of most of her quarrels.

quotations.text: “Marilla, isn’t it nice to think that tomorrow is a new day with no mistakes in it yet?”
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: The evening of the liniment cake, after the minister and his wife have gone home.
quotations.analysis: She offers the consolation to Marilla, not to herself, which is the first sign of the adult Anne. ‘Yet’ keeps the sentence honest: it admits that tomorrow will also be full of mistakes, and proposes only that they have not happened.

quotations.text: “I must do it. My honour is at stake,” said Anne solemnly. “I shall walk that ridgepole, Diana, or perish in the attempt. If I am killed you are to have my pearl bead ring.”
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Josie Pye has dared her to walk the ridgepole of the Barrys’ kitchen roof.
quotations.analysis: The language of chivalric romance is applied to a dare from a girl she dislikes, and the will disposing of a pearl bead ring is the exact measure of what Anne owns. The narrator then notes drily that walking ridgepoles is not a thing in which imagination helps you out much — the book’s clearest statement of where the gift stops.

quotations.text: “Yes, it’s green,” moaned Anne. “I thought nothing could be as bad as red hair. But now I know it’s ten times worse to have green hair.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Confessing to Marilla after buying hair dye from a pedlar.
quotations.analysis: The comedy depends on a genuinely painful fact established twenty chapters earlier: the hair is the one thing about herself Anne has never been able to redescribe. Her consolation afterwards — that a wicked act should at least be wicked to some purpose — is the closest the novel comes to a theology of mistakes.

quotations.text: There are so many things in this room and all so splendid that there is no scope for imagination. That is one consolation when you are poor⁠—there are so many more things you can imagine about.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: In Miss Barry’s spare room in Charlottetown, on the visit that follows the hotel concert.
quotations.analysis: The novel’s economics stated in two sentences, and by the person they apply to: imagination is described as a compensation for not having things. It is also a considerable piece of tact, delivered in a velvet-carpeted room belonging to a rich woman who is listening.

quotations.text: I’m not a bit changed⁠—not really. I’m only just pruned down and branched out.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Sitting on Marilla’s lap at Green Gables, home from Queen’s, after Marilla has said she seems grown up and different.
quotations.analysis: The metaphor is taken from the orchard outside the window, which is the register Marilla can actually hear — Anne has learned to translate. It also concedes more than it admits: pruning is a loss of growth carried out deliberately, and the last chapters will require exactly that.

quotations.text: “Well now, I’d rather have you than a dozen boys, Anne,” said Matthew patting her hand. “Just mind you that⁠—rather than a dozen boys.
quotations.speaker: Matthew Cuthbert
quotations.context: Walking back with the cows on the last evening of his life, after Anne has said she wishes she had been the boy they sent for.
quotations.analysis: The sentence answers the clerical error of Chapter 1 directly, and Matthew repeats it because he knows he is bad at saying things. Montgomery places it the evening before his death, so that the novel’s one explicit declaration of love is also the last thing he manages to do.

quotations.text: It’s never been easy for me to say things out of my heart, but at times like this it’s easier. I love you as dear as if you were my own flesh and blood and you’ve been my joy and comfort ever since you came to Green Gables.
quotations.speaker: Marilla Cuthbert
quotations.context: The night after Matthew’s funeral, hearing Anne crying in her room.
quotations.analysis: Marilla explains why she can speak before she speaks, which is characteristic: the confession is prefaced by an account of her own reticence. ‘As dear as if’ preserves the fact that Anne is not her flesh and blood, and the novel’s whole argument about who belongs to whom is settled on that conjunction.

quotations.text: When I left Queen’s my future seemed to stretch out before me like a straight road. I thought I could see along it for many a milestone. Now there is a bend in it. I don’t know what lies around the bend, but I’m going to believe that the best does.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Telling Marilla that she has given up the Avery scholarship and will teach at Carmody instead.
quotations.analysis: The image is the opposite of the one she began with: a road she cannot see along is now preferable to a road she can. Note the verb, ‘I’m going to believe’, which makes optimism an act of will, and answers everyone who has called her a case.

quotations.text: God’s in his heaven, all’s right with the world,
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: The last line of the novel, whispered at the gable window.
quotations.analysis: The line is Browning’s, sung by a child in a play about a village that is not in fact all right, and Montgomery hands it to a girl whose horizons have just closed in. The quotation is the point: Anne ends the book borrowing somebody else’s certainty and choosing to mean it.

quotations.text: I think some kinds of sewing would be nice; but there’s no scope for imagination in patchwork.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Set to sew red and white diamonds by Marilla, who believes in useful work.
quotations.analysis: The phrase that began as a description of a railway platform has become a general test she applies to everything, from cookery to algebra. It is also a joke about the novel’s own form: a book made of small self-contained episodes stitched into a pattern is complaining about patchwork.

timeline.label: Lucy Maud Montgomery born at Clifton, Prince Edward Island
timeline.detail: The village now called New London, a few miles from Cavendish.

timeline.label: Her mother dies; she is sent to her grandparents at Cavendish
timeline.detail: The household of an elderly couple and a child not quite their own is the one the novel rearranges.

timeline.label: Montgomery begins the novel
timeline.detail: She started writing in June, after months of what she called spade work on character and incident.

timeline.label: Contract with L. C. Page and Company
timeline.detail: Signed on 22 April, with the Boston firm that would publish the book and its sequels.

timeline.label: Anne of Green Gables published
timeline.detail: The first edition appeared in June; Montgomery recorded receiving her copies on the 20th.

timeline.label: First translation, into Swedish
timeline.detail: A Swedish edition appeared within a year, the beginning of an international readership.

timeline.label: Montgomery marries and leaves the Island
timeline.detail: She moved to Ontario as a Presbyterian minister’s wife, and wrote most of the Anne books away from Cavendish.

timeline.label: First film version
timeline.detail: A silent adaptation, now lost, made a decade after publication.

timeline.label: L. C. Page issues a reset and altered edition
timeline.detail: L. C. Page issued a newly set and slightly altered edition, which is why the 1908 printing matters as a base text.

timeline.label: Montgomery dies in Toronto
timeline.detail: She was buried at Cavendish, within sight of the landscape the novel renames.

timeline.label: The Canadian television adaptation
timeline.detail: Kevin Sullivan’s version fixed the novel’s appearance for a generation of readers and made Prince Edward Island a destination.

places.name: Cavendish, Prince Edward Island
places.note: The village Montgomery grew up in, and the source — not the map — of Avonlea.

places.name: New London, Prince Edward Island
places.note: Clifton, where Montgomery was born in 1874.

places.name: Charlottetown
places.note: The provincial capital, where Anne boards for her year at Queen’s Academy.

places.name: Gulf of St Lawrence shore
places.note: The north-shore coast and dunes that make Avonlea a triangular peninsula with water on two sides.

places.name: Boston
places.note: Home of L. C. Page and Company, whose 1908 printing fixed the novel’s American spelling and punctuation.

criticalViews.summary: One long-standing reading holds that the real development in the book is the guardian’s: Anne is much the same person in Chapter 38 as in Chapter 3, while Marilla moves from thinking a girl useless to saying she loves her as dear as her own flesh and blood.
criticalViews.counter: It underrates what Anne gives up in the last chapter, which is a genuine loss and a genuine decision.

criticalViews.position: An orphan story with the economics left in
criticalViews.summary: Read beside the period’s home-child schemes, the opening is not sentimental at all: children were placed on farms as labour, and the novel’s first crisis is that the wrong kind of labour has arrived. Mrs Blewett is the book’s reminder of what the ordinary outcome looked like.
criticalViews.counter: The novel then declines to follow the economics, since Green Gables can afford a child who is not useful.

criticalViews.position: A book about imagination and its limits
criticalViews.summary: Criticism has often focused on how carefully Montgomery balances the gift against the damage: the same faculty that renames a pond produces the Haunted Wood, the hair dye and the sinking flat. Growing up in this novel means learning when to switch it off, not learning to do without it.
criticalViews.counter: The final chapters can be read as a loss of nerve, in which a girl’s ambition is disciplined into a smaller life and called contentment.

criticalViews.summary: The novel’s afterlife has made Prince Edward Island a literary destination, with a preserved farmhouse and a tourist trade that lives off a fictional village. Discussion of the book now has to include what happens when a landscape is recognised chiefly through somebody’s imaginary names for it.
criticalViews.counter: Montgomery herself distinguished source from setting, and never claimed Avonlea was a map of Cavendish.

essayQuestions.question: Whose education does the novel actually describe?
essayQuestions.focus: Anne, Marilla and the direction of change
plan: Establish what Anne is like in Chapters 2 to 4, and see how much of it survives to Chapter 38.
Track Marilla instead: the decision in Chapter 6, the amethyst brooch, the silent pride at the pass list, the confession in Chapter 37.
Use free indirect style as evidence — the narration enters Marilla’s thoughts at exactly the points she refuses to speak.
Consider Matthew as the constant against which both are measured, and what his death forces each of them to say.
Conclude on the last chapter: who has given something up, and who has learned to say something.

essayQuestions.question: How does Montgomery use Anne’s imagination?
essayQuestions.focus: Naming, invention and the cost of both
plan: Begin with naming as the only power available to a child with no possessions: Cordelia, the e, the Lake of Shining Waters.
Show imagination working as protection in Chapter 4 — she will imagine she is staying — and as sociability with Diana.
Turn to the damage: the Haunted Wood she cannot walk through, the pedlar’s dye, the leaky flat and Elaine.
Examine the narrator’s dry line about ridgepoles, which states the limit explicitly.
End with the last two chapters, where imagination becomes a decision to believe something about a road she cannot see.

essayQuestions.question: ‘A comic novel that turns serious too late.’ How far do you agree?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, episode and the final chapters
plan: Describe the episodic method: each chapter a complete disaster with a lesson attached.
Show how the comedy accumulates consequence — the liniment cake gains an ally, the dyed hair loses a plait, the slate makes a rival.
Read the bank failure and Matthew’s death as an intrusion of a different kind of plot, with money and health at stake.
Assess the last chapter’s refusals: no scholarship, no reversal, no rescue, and a career redefined at Carmody.
Decide whether the ending is a change of key or the point the earlier chapters were preparing for.

essayQuestions.question: What does the novel show about Avonlea as a community?
plan: Start with the first page: a brook, a window and a village that knows what everyone is sowing.
Use Mrs Rachel Lynde’s quarrel and reconciliation as the test case for how the village handles a newcomer.
Weigh the institutions the book records — Sunday school, the manse, the Debating Club, the concert, the pass list in the paper.
Consider Mrs Blewett and the asylum as the alternatives lying just outside Avonlea’s charity.
Conclude with Chapter 38, where the same neighbours who judged Anne are the reason she can stay.

discussionQuestions: Matthew says seven words in Chapter 3 and changes the course of the book. What does the novel gain by making its most decisive character almost silent?
Anne refuses Gilbert’s apology for five years. Is the novel on her side?
The book insists that imagination saves Anne and also causes most of her disasters. Can it be both?
Marilla can only say that she loves Anne once Matthew is dead. What does the novel suggest about how such households work?
Is giving up the Avery scholarship a sacrifice, a defeat, or a choice? Does the last page persuade you?

related.why: Another Edwardian book in which a family’s money vanishes and children have to make a new life in an unfamiliar countryside.
The earlier orphan story this one answers: a plain, clever, unwanted girl who insists on the value of her own judgement.
Montgomery writing about an adult woman’s escape from respectability, with the comedy sharper and the constraint more explicit.
The other great book about a talkative girl arguing with adults who will not follow her reasoning.
A child raised by hand in somebody else’s household, and the same question about what gratitude is supposed to cost.
